paper_title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent. 1. Introduction Video generation models are now strong enough to tell stories [33, 45, 51, 58], and agents that plan shots, track characters, and check results keep multi-shot videos consistent across scenes [26, 60, 62, 68, 86]. Live streaming, games, and world models need different kind of generator: autoregressive (AR), few-step models that stream long videos in real time and accept new prompts while they play [6, 19, 23, 28, 40, 47, 74, 77]. These generators have no agent. Their memory is the key/value (KV) cache: an attention sink that keeps the first frames [65, 74] and short window of recent frames. Older content is forgotten, and what is kept is the models own output, so wrong face or lost object is copied forward [11, 28].

sections.content: 1 real-time video cannot wait. live session imposes four constraints that offline agent systems do not face: (C1) the future is unknown, so memory for shot must be ready before its prompt arrives; (C2) there is no length limit, so GPU memory must stay constant; (C3) the deadline is hard, so the video never waits for memory construction: planning, drawing, and prefilling must stay hidden, and once prompt arrives only quick choice among prepared memory is affordable; (C4) there is no rollback, so played shots cannot be repaired. Existing video agents rely on what live session lacks: they read the whole script (C1), plan each shot while generation waits (C3), and inspect and regenerate failed shots (C4) [26, 55, 60]. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory that gives real-time AR generators longterm memory without slowing them down  (Fig. 1)  . Asynchronous memory: memory agent runs on its own GPUs and commits the memory for shot before prompt is revealed, and an auxiliary GPU prefills it into the generators KV cache, so the agents time is hidden behind generation. Open-loop entity memory: the agent reads only revealed prompts, never the video, so video errors are not written back. It keeps text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene, composes them into global image and shot memory that enter the frozen generator as attention sinks, and appends text cards of the entities prompt names. Learning what to remember: before the next prompt is known, the agent must choose which entities to draw. We train small language model for this with reinforcement learning (RL), using hindsight reward whose image term is calibrated using downstream video outcomes. We also build LongStory-Online, 25 stories (857 shots, about 150 minutes) with hidden annotations, where prompts are revealed one shot at time and every shot is generated exactly once. On LongLive-2.0 [6], Agentic LongLive improves persistent state, protagonist identity, and location on scene changes by 26 to 45 points, adding about 1% generation time on H100, and streams faster than real time on one 8B200 node in BF16 (34.3 FPS). Its image quality stays flat over 14-minute stories, its identity gains carry over to two few-step MiniMax-H3 generators [43, 45], with LongLive-H3 also in real time on B200 (1.45), and RL lets an 8B planner replace the 35B planner. We contribute: an asynchronous agentic memory system that hides agent latency behind real-time generation with constant GPU memory and no length limit, to our knowledge the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent; an open-loop two-layer memory as attention sinks of frozen AR generator, with entity cards in the prompt; an RL recipe with video-calibrated reward that teaches small LLM what to remember, and the LongStoryOnline benchmark. LongStory-Online has 25 stories, 857 shots, and about 150 minutes of video: nine stories written by hand (211 shots) and sixteen LongStory-Hard stories designed by an LLM with states accumulated by code (646 shots). Stories have more entities than memory slots, long absences and revisits, persistent changes (clothing, dirt, damage, assembly), and prompts that overturn earlier inferences. Each shot has hidden annotation of entities, persistent states, and location, frozen before any method was run. Prompts are terse, like real user input: place or person is described once, and later prompts use names or back in the kitchen. Baselines. LongLive-2.0 [6] shares our backbone and keeps its built-in memory: sinks on the first chunk of the video and of each shot, and KV window carried across shots. Four open AR models on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, Self-Forcing [28], CausVid [77], Causal-Forcing [89], and Rolling Forcing [40], run one rollout per story with the prompt switched at each shot. Self-Forcing breaks down within minutes, as in its official code (83% of its shots have severe artifacts), so we do not rank it. On MiniMax-H3 [45], we test two few-step chunked-AR generators: RAVEN [43] and LongLive-H3. We distill LongLive-H3 from MiniMaxH3 by causal distribution matching distillation (DMD) [76] on prompts alone. It generates video and audio in chunks of about 0.7 s, each attending to the text, the first chunk, and the two previous chunks (App. C). Without memory, each 8 shot is generated from its prompt alone. second baseline carries K/V across shots as LongLive-2.0 does (App. C). The non-real-time systems StoryMem [83] and StoryEngine [60], an offline variant of ours, SkyReelsV2 [5], and all baseline adaptations are in App. F. Metrics. VLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash), different from every model of the real-time agent and of RL training, compares four frames of each shot with its annotation: State (persistent attributes correct), Identity (the visible protagonist matches its description), and Location (on scene changes). Same protagonist compares each shot whose plan shows the protagonist with the methods first shot of it (0 if the protagonist is missing). Revisit rates whether return shows the same place as the last visit and counts only returns where both shots are at their planned place [60]. We also report VBench imaging quality [29] and the share of shots with severe artifacts. Framing, imaging drift [40], and ArcFace face identity (MIR [60]) are in App. and H. Rejudging agrees on 9296% of decisions. As the same model also wrote the Hard stories, second judge from another family (GPT-5.5) re-judged 14 runs and confirms 87 of the 94 significant comparisons, with no sign flip (App. E). Automated-metric differences quoted in the text are differences of table entries, significant unless noted (a storyclustered bootstrap 95% interval excludes zero). Implementation. LongLive-2.0 runs Wan2.2-TI2V5B [58] in BF16 with 4 steps and 10.5 shots. The agent checks images and routes scenes with Qwen3.635B-A3B [52] and draws with FLUX.2-klein-4B [2], each on one H100. In the full system, the RL planner (Qwen3-8B [73] with LoRA [24]) writes the memory on third H100. Without RL, the 35B model also plans. The full system thus uses six H100s (DiT 1, auxiliary 2, agent 3), against two for LongLive-2.0 alone (DiT and asynchronous decoder). Memory streams come from the live agent against stand-in generator with the same shot time (zero lag on 9799% of shots) and are replayed into each generator, pixel-identical to live run. On LongLive2.0, rows with the RL planner pair each of three planners, trained with different seeds, with one video seed. 3.2. Main results Same backbone. On LongLive-2.0, our system and the built-in memory share the generator and the prompts, so the comparison isolates memory. The full system improves all five consistency columns (Tab. 1). State accuracy rises by 26.3 points, and revisit consistency from 15.0% to 55.4%. Imaging quality also improves and, unlike with the built-in memory, does not decay over story  (Fig. 6)  . The cost is about 1% generation time on H100 (Sec. 3.3). Sections 3.4 and 3.5 separate the contributions of memory images, scene routing, entity cards, and the RL planner. Other real-time AR models. The four Wan2.1 models run smaller backbone at lower resolution, so this comparison mixes backbone and memory. Without our memory, LongLive-2.0 already leads them in state and location, but not in identity, same protagonist, or revisit (e.g. 44.1% vs. 59.8% identity for Causal-Forcing). With our memory it leads in all five consistency columns (Tab. 1, top, all significant). Rolling Forcing has the highest imaging quality (0.748) but rarely follows scene change (33.1% location). Other backbones. On the MiniMax-H3 generators, our memory mainly improves identity: it rises from 61.0% to 98.0% on RAVEN and from 58.2% to 96.8% on LongLiveH3. State, same protagonist, and revisit rise with it, and location stays at or above the level without memory. Without memory, severe artifacts are rare (0.5% and 0.9%) because each shot starts from noise, so errors cannot carry over. sections.content: The appendix first reviews related work (Sec. A) and then follows the order of the experiments: system and speed (Sec. B, for Sec. 3.3), memory design (Sec. C, for Sec. 3.4), memory planner (Sec. D, for Sec. 3.5), benchmark and metrics (Sec. E), and baselines (Sec. F), followed by tests of the agent on robot video models (Sec. G), by entity evolution, failure cases, and limitations (Sec. H), and by the human preference study (Sec. I). Several analyses in this appendix evaluate the image memory without entity cards. There, image system denotes the image memory with LLM scene routing and the RL planner (the RL planners imagememory row of Tab. 3), and full system adds the cards. A. Related Work Real-time AR video generation. Diffusion Forcing [4] and CausVid [77] make video diffusion causal. Self Forcing [28] and its successors [11, 40, 43] close the traintest gap with self rollouts and few-step distillation. MAGI1 [53], SkyReels-V2 [5], Krea Realtime [34], APT2 [38], and StreamDiT [32] scale this up. To run without length limit, these models keep fixed window of recent frames and an attention sink [65]. Rolling Sink [35] keeps this cache close to what the model saw in training, without retraining, so rollouts stay stable far beyond the training horizon. LongLive [74] adds frame sink and KV re-caching for prompt switches. LongLive-2.0 [6] adds multi-shot sinks and parallel inference, and LongLive-Plug [75] distills few-step and long-video LoRAs once and plugs them into other models of the same backbone family. Other works pack or route longer context [3, 63, 84], split the cache into sink, archive, and working banks [82], or retrieve earlier frames by the current prompt [30]. In all of them, memory lives inside the generator and is built from its own frames (closed loop). Our memory lives outside the generator and is written by an agent from the prompts alone. Agents and memory for multi-shot video. Agentic storytelling systems write scripts, draw keyframes, and repair shots with VLM feedback [25, 26, 55, 59, 60, 62, 68, 71, 86]. The closest, StoryEngine [60], keeps structured entity states and canonical references. All of them run offline: they see the full script and can select or regenerate shots. Concurrent works bring agents closer to streaming. AgiWorld [15] links planning agent and video world model through shared spatial memory. Wizard [64] controls real-time game world model with VLM agent that turns instructions into programs over scene geometry. AgiWorld does not report real-time operation, and Wizards agent edits scene geometry and symbolic game state, not image memory. To our knowledge, ours is the first realtime video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent: the video never waits for the agent, and the whole system streams faster than playback. Other methods keep memory inside the model. They carry keyframes or long context across shots [20, 44, 66, 83] or index past frames by pose and time [36, 67, 79], so their memory comes from generated pixels. Reference-to-video models [13, 17, 41, 45] inject fixed set of reference images. We instead decide what to store and update it during the session, and our memory images can serve as references. Asynchronous agents and learned memory. Robot systems run slow planner beside fast controller [1, 46, 56, 57], and LLM agents overlap thinking with waiting [9, 10]. Our slow agent instead must commit versioned memory to separate real-time generator before deadline. LLM agents also learn what to store [8, 49, 70, 72, 78, 88], and RL tunes prompts for image and video models [7, 21, 31, 61] with learned judges [22, 39, 69]. We combine the two. One LoRA-tuned planner writes the structured memory and the text that the frozen generator reads, and its image reward is calibrated on real videos. B. Asynchronous System and Speed Measurement. DiT FPS is the number of frames divided by denoising time, excluding VAE decoding, as in LongLive-2.0 [6]. End-to-end FPS divides frames by wall-clock time including decoding, memory prefill, shotboundary swaps, and waiting. The real-time factor is video seconds over wall-clock seconds. Overhead is the relative increase in wall-clock time over the base generator on the same hardware, prompts, and video length. Each method is warmed up and loaded once. Events (start and end of each DiT chunk, end of each decode, memory commit, prefill done, boundary swap) are timestamped after cuda.synchronize, and all numbers come from one timing log per run. DiT throughput varies by 12% across GPUs, so overheads within 2% are treated as noise. The H100 timing runs on LongLive-2.0 have no entity cards, which the agent writes off the critical path. All H3 rows, with and without memory, use the same H3 prompts, and the routing decisions of the H3 rows are made on them. LongLive-H3. We obtain LongLive-H3 from MiniMaxH3 by causal distribution matching distillation (DMD) [76], with the chunking and few-step schedule of RAVEN [43]. The frozen, bidirectional MiniMax-H3 serves as the realscore teacher. The student is LoRA of rank 128 on the frozen backbone, and second rank-128 LoRA serves as the fake-score model, trained by flow matching on the students own rollouts. The student is trained with the normalized DMD surrogate, and fake-score and student updates alternate 5:1 after 50 fake-score-only warm-up updates. Training uses prompts only, without real video or audio: 1,024 original single-shot prompts from SMD-H3T2VA-100K and 256 multi-shot prompts that we rebuilt from SMD. Training clips have 124 frames at 1344768 and 24 fps with jointly generated 32 kHz stereo audio, i.e. 37 video latents and 207 audio latents per channel. Each clip is split into eight chunks, seven of 5 video latents (about 0.7 s) and 2-latent tail, with the audio split at the same boundaries. Attention is block-causal: each chunk attends to the text, the first chunk as sink, the two previous chunks, and itself, and earlier chunks are fed as clean context at clock 0.999. We train on 32 GB300 GPUs with global batch of 64 (2 per GPU), learning rates of 2 106 for the student and 105 for the fake-score model, and EMA decay 0.99. The released checkpoint is the EMA after 200 student updates (1,000 fake-score updates). At inference, LongLive-H3 takes 3 steps per chunk and generates 8 shots (192 frames), longer than its training clips. With KV cache that reproduces its chunked sampler, shot takes 50.2 on one H100 (116 on A100), and all quality results use this one-GPU path. This holds for 349 of 857 shots (41%), with prompt written once. Each of these shots scores (rating1)/4 against the methods first shot of the protagonist (four frames of each shot, compared on face, hair, build, age, species, and markings, while clothing, dirt, and pose may change) and 0 if the shot judge does not see the protagonist. The reference shot itself is excluded. Because the shots are fixed by the plan, video that loses the protagonist or breaks down cannot score by showing the protagonist less often, and because pairs at any place and distance count, carrying the previous shots pixels forward does not help either. Revisit rates whether returning shot shows the same place as the last visit and counts return only if both shots are judged to be at their planned location, as the geometric place consistency of StoryEngine [60] counts only shots in the right scene, so model that stays in one place cannot score by looking the same. Face identity (MIR). MIR follows StoryEngine exactly (its App. D.8). It takes four evenly spaced frames per shot, including the first and last, and keeps InsightFace buffalo detections at 640640 with score 0.55. In shot order, each embedding joins the cluster with the most similar mean if the cosine is 0.45 and otherwise starts new one, and single-detection clusters are dropped. MIR is the minimum over clusters of the mean cosine between detections from different shots, and 0 when no cluster spans two shots. We report MIR here rather than in Tab. 1 because it measures faces only (two of our 25 protagonists are an animal and robot), it rewards videos that repeat nearly the same frames across shots, and it does not penalize video that breaks down (Self-Forcing 0.400). Same protagonist is used in the main paper. With our memory, MIR is higher on both MiniMax-H3 generators (Tab. E3): by +0.005 (RAVEN) and +0.049 (LongLive-H3) over the 25 stories, and by +0.051 and +0.070 on the nine hand-written stories, though none of these differences is significant. Among StoryMem, StoryEngine, and our offline variants, the offline variant on H3 Ref2VA has the highest MIR (0.403 and 0.455, against 0.385 and 0.423 for StoryEngine). On LongLive-2.0, image memory lowers MIR from 0.334 to 0.191. LongLive-2.0s built-in memory carries the previous shots K/V and so keeps some faces across adjacent shots, which MIR rewards. ArcFace embeddings of small generated faces are also noisy (cosine 0.10.3 between faces of the same shot below 60 px, 0.60.8 above 100 px), which lowers MIR for every model at these resolutions. The other systems drift by 0.003 (StoryMem) to 0.064 (SkyReels-V2), and RAVEN by 0.009 without and 0.003 with our memory. F. Baselines Real-time baselines. Rolling Forcing supports single prompt, so we split generation per shot, re-cache KV at prompt switches as in LongLive [74], and wrap RoPE after 1,024 positions (stories reach 1,764 latent frames). It takes 19.3 per shot. The other Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B models use the same protocol: one continuous rollout per story, 42 latent frames per shot (10.310.5 at 16 fps), only the current shot prompt, and one seed set before the first shot. Shot 0 of every model is identical to its official inference. Self-Forcing uses the official sampler (4 steps, 3-frame blocks) with the repositorys rolling KV cache of 21 frames (its training context) and no sink. Cached frames are recomputed under each new prompt as for Rolling Forcing, and RoPE wraps after 1,024 frames (18.2 per shot). Causal-Forcing is run with the authors long-video checkpoint, which uses the Rolling Forcing inference code (17.4 per shot). Its 5second chunkwise checkpoint, run like Self-Forcing, breaks down within about two shots (87.6% of its shots have severe artifacts). CausVid uses the repositorys long-video 23 script, with rollouts of up to 21 latent frames, each started from 3 overlap frames, and 3 steps. Rollouts never cross shot boundary, so new prompt starts the next rollout and re-encodes the overlap under that prompt (13.4 per shot). SkyReels-V2 uses DF-1.3B-540P at 960544 with official settings (30 steps, guidance 6, TeaCache 0.3): shot 0 is text-to-video and each later shot is video extension of 160 frames (10 at 16 fps) conditioned on the last 17 frames, with its own prompt (87.6 per shot, one seed). The model then continues for 5.3 under the instruction followed by the camera moves back and the whole scene is visible again. Our memory is built from the first frame before the close-up: the 35B model of the main text names the target object, returns its box, and writes card of at most 20 words. The first frame and crop around the box enter the sink as still blocks, and the card is appended to the prompt. Without memory, the model turns to different scene. With our memory, the object is back in 96.4% of the last frames (60.7% without), and the same-object score rises by 2.36 points, in all seven scenes. Given the same observation, pictures, and card as references, the offline MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA (50 steps) keeps the object even without memory but continues into different room. Our memory restores the scene (scene consistency from 2.9 to 7.0 of 10, +4.1) and raises the same-object score by 1.36 points. Long-horizon robot tasks. Generated robot data needs long videos in which the robot works through many steps while parts of the scene leave the view and come back. We take the first frames of 30 validation clips of RoVidX [14], which cover one and two arms, grippers and hands, and head-mounted and fixed cameras. For each first frame, Gemini 3.8 Flash drafted script of eight 8 instructions (64 in total), which we then edited by hand. The first instructions finish the clips own task. Each script then hides one or two things and brings each back one to four instructions later. head camera turns away and back (20 return moments), or drawer, fridge, box, or lid is closed and reopened, or an object is covered and uncovered (21 moments). An instruction that brings something back never describes it, for example pull the top left drawer open again and reach in for what you put there, so only memory can tell the generator what to show. Each segment continues from the last frame of the previous one, so that the 64 video is meant to be one continuous take, although the generator can still cut on its own. Without memory, this frame is all that the generator knows about the scene. Unlike the main text, where the memory for shot must be ready before its prompt arrives (C1), each instruction here is available one segment before it plays, as in scripted robot task, and the agent uses it to choose pictures and rewrite it. This section therefore tests observation-based memory on robot videos, not C1. Agent. Unlike the open-loop agent of the main text, this agent observes the video, because robot acts in one continuous scene rather than in separate shots. Where an object ends up, or whether drawer is still open, depends on the generated video rather than on the script, so the memory has to be read from that video. As in the close-up test, it is an observation-based variant: its memory pictures are frames that the robots camera has already shown, or crops of them, so it needs no image model. After each segment, the agent looks at three of its frames. It describes the view, lists the visible objects with their position and look, and records whether each container is open or closed and what it holds. It also picks frame to keep, frame that shows the inside of an open container, and boxes for up to two objects. Code turns these observations into two parts of memory. record of objects and containers keeps an object that was put into closed container as hidden inside it. bank of pictures holds one view per segment, container interiors, and the newest crop of each object, each with caption and the segment it comes from. Before each segment, router answers one narrow question about the next instruction: does something come back into view, because the camera turns back, container is reopened, cover is lifted, or an object is taken out? It agrees with the scripts annotations in 188 of 210 segments. Only when something comes back, the agent sees the bank as thumbnails and lists every picture of the returning place, container, or object. It pins the newest matching view and the newest close view (at most two pictures, Fig. G1) and rewrites the instruction so that it names what comes back and how it looked when last seen. Otherwise it pins nothing and only rewrites the instruction to name the objects with their look. Pinning only on returns matters: pictures pinned in almost every segment make the generator restore old states, for example tube put into drawer reappears on the cabinet. The agent was developed on one of the 30 episodes and then kept fixed for all runs. Generators. Table G2 uses two generators from earlier sections: FastH3-Omni, as in the real-time runs of Sec. The pinned pictures and then the latest frame enter the sink, Real time and parallelism. The closed loop still runs in parallel with generation. The agent observes decoded frames and writes memory while the generator renders on other GPUs, and this memory enters only when the next segment starts, never within segment. How early the agent can observe depends on the generator. FastH3-Omni is bidirectional and returns segment only when all of it is decoded, so when segment starts, the newest frame that the agent has seen is 8 old. LongLive-H3 generates segment chunk by chunk and decodes each chunk as it is generated, so the agent can observe the first half of segment i1 while the second half is still being generated, and the newest frame it has seen is 4 old. We timed both loops on six episodes, with the generator on eight B200 GPUs and the agent on two A100 GPUs. With FastH3-Omni, the agent (2.3 on average) never makes the generator wait. With the last decoded frame passed straight to the next request, each 8 segment takes 7.6 on average, and every segment is ready before it is due to play. With LongLive-H3 on five of the GPUs, the first half of segment is decoded 3.3 after the segment starts and the agent needs 1.9 s, so the generator usually waits about 0.5 for it at the boundary. The loop still runs in real time, at 5.8 per 8 segment on average (at most 7.7 s), because generation is faster than playback. We time LongLive-H3 but do not score it. It is not trained on robot videos, and with or without memory it does not keep the input robot, whose grippers, for example, turn into humanoid hands early in the video. Results. Table G2 compares whole 64 videos at the 41 return moments and over all 210 generated segments. Our memory raises the consistency of what comes back with its last appearance from 3.98 to 5.59 with FastH3-Omni (+1.61, second seed +1.66) and from 3.54 to 5.51 with H3 Ref2VA (+1.98). The hidden thing is back in view at 76% instead of 44% of the return moments with FastH3Omni, and back with the same identity and position at 56% instead of 20% (H3 Ref2VA: 44% instead of 5%). Camera returns gain the most (+2.55 and +2.35), because the pinned view shows the whole place. Reopened containers gain less (+0.71, not significant, and +1.62): in four of the nine FastH3-Omni reopenings that score below 5, the generator never opens the lid, lifts the cover, or takes the object out, which memory cannot fix. Task progress stays level (neither difference significant), and segments in which nothing comes back revert to an earlier state about as often as without memory, because nothing is pinned there. The pinned views also show the robot, so its look stays closer to the input image (same-robot score 7.84 vs. 7.05 with FastH3-Omni and 7.36 vs. 6.53 with H3 Ref2VA). Second, the generator can follow pinned picture too literally. When the pinned view shows an earlier open state, FastH3-Omni may briefly reopen lid that was closed, and it sometimes jumps to the pinned frame instead of turning toward it. Third, the robot itself drifts slowly over the minute, for example from gripper to hand. With memory, its identity score is at most 5 in 21.9% of segment ends (30.5% without memory). H. Entity Evolution and Limitations Entity evolution. Figure H1 shows how the entity images of the RL planners memory change over story: new version is drawn as an edit of the previous image when prompt states persistent change, and it shows only persistent attributes on plain backdrop, with pose and action left to the next prompt. Failure cases and limitations. Memory follows the story up to the previous prompt, because it is built before the next prompt arrives (C3). Two cases follow from this. persistent change that the current prompt states for the first time, such as character shaving, is not yet in the memory images of that shot, which can keep the earlier look until the agent has drawn the change for the following shots. reIf called place comes with the picture of its last visit. character has changed since, the cards state the new look, but an attribute that no card names can follow the earlier picture until the place is drawn again. Re-injecting updated memory within shot, once its prompt has arrived, would address both cases and is left to future work. Framing. For every shot, the judge also decides whether the shot size, camera angle, and main subject agree with the planned camera and content (framing match in the judge prompt of Sec. E). Re-judging agrees on 94.8% of shots, and the second judge agrees with κ = 0.71. None of the compared works scores framing. On LongLive-2.0, framing rises with our full system from 58.5% to 65.9% of shots (three seeds), but planned close-ups, quarter of all shots, fall from 75.5% to 63.7%. Memory images show whole entities in medium or wide views and pull the generator toward that shot size, so 78% of the remaining misses are rendered as medium shots. Memory is built before the prompt (C3), so it cannot be drawn at the shot size of the coming shot, whereas StoryEngine and our offline variants, which draw keyframe or references after each prompt, reach 7495% framing. Long text also competes with camera words: cards for every injected member cost 22.4 framing points alone and 11.9 with images, whereas cards for the entities that the prompt names cost none (0.7 with the 35B planner, not significant). Thirty-two volunteers from our research community took part, recruited by convenience sampling. Each judged ten stories of LongStory-Online: five comparisons on LongLive-2.0 (its built-in memory vs. our full system) and five on LongLive-H3 (independent shots, K/V carried across shots, and our full system), with the videos of Tab. 1 at seed 0. comparison shows four shots spread over the story (first, one third, two thirds, and last), with the anonymous versions side by side in rotating order and short note on what happens between the shots (Fig. I1). Method names and memory images are not shown. For each of four criteria, identity consistency, persistent state, location correctness, and visual quality, participants pick the best version, mark tie, or answer Cannot judge (missing visual evidence or playback failure). Ethics. Participation was voluntary and anonymous and could be stopped at any time. Every response includes informed consent, and the form stored no personal data. No formal IRB review was conducted, as the study was minimal-risk perceptual evaluation of generated videos. Results.
